set.plain: Do autopsies and drug tests change which deaths count as drug deaths? At one autopsy centre in North Carolina (2016 to 2021), investigators suspected that 2,719 deaths were drug deaths. After a full autopsy and drug tests, about 1 in 10 of them had another cause, such as a blood clot or a burst blood vessel in the brain. This is an upper limit for the suspected deaths, because it includes deaths where tests found no drug at all. Of 237 deaths nobody suspected, drug tests showed that about half were drug deaths. The authors say that most deaths would have been put down correctly from the scene, an outside examination of the body and full drug tests, without an autopsy. Testing differs a lot: in 2018, about 1 in 9 US death investigation offices said they had no access to drug testing (some may send deaths elsewhere for testing), and small offices had it less often than big ones. Medical examiners' guidance says to do an autopsy whenever a drug death is suspected, but the error figure it gives comes mostly from autopsy studies of all kinds of deaths. This rests mainly on one centre in one US state.
set.magnitude: North Carolina centre 2016–2021 (Hancock et al., 2024): suspected before autopsy 2,719 of 2,956; non-drug final cause in 265 (9.75%; editors' Wilson 95% interval 8.7% to 10.9%), an upper limit for external examination with toxicology among the suspected deaths only; not suspected 237, drug-related final cause shown by toxicology in 115 (48.5%, 42.2% to 54.9%, editors' calculation); printed sensitivity 95.52%, specificity 31.52%. Second-hand in the same paper (not read): 11% to 13% of suspected drug deaths with no drug found and another cause; 75% to 80% correct on cause and manner without internal examination in 60 selected cases. US 2018 census (Smiley-McDonald et al., 2025), 1,320 offices: toxicology access 82.6% (in-house 5.9%, outside 76.7%), none 11.2%, not needed 6.2%; large offices 96.4%, small 75.1%; coroner or non-physician named among those deciding testing by 64.7% of offices; screening 53.9% of 1,326, laboratory confirmation 95.1% of 709; shares of offices, self-reported. Nine US states 2019–2021 (Lundberg et al., 2026): full or partial autopsy recorded about 67%, opioid test 79%, alcohol test 76% of 55,430. Second-hand: Kentucky gabapentin 2.9% (2013) to 17% (2014), routine testing from July 2014 (Slavova et al., 2019). Kentucky coroners 2016, 48 of 120: more toxicology 58.3%, more autopsies 35.4%, self-reported (Quesinberry et al., 2019). Norway 2007–2009: no autopsy, adjusted odds ratio 2.66 (1.42–4.98) for being counted only by the cause-of-death register (Amundsen, 2017). NAME's 20% to 30% error figure is from general autopsy studies and a mortality data brief (Davis et al., 2020).

evidence_set: As the review reports (citing Hargrove et al., 2018): after routine gabapentin testing was introduced in Kentucky in July 2014, the prevalence of gabapentin among drug overdose decedents rose from 2.9% in 2013 to 17% in 2014, which the review attributes to the new testing; the authors warn that gradual improvements in procedures produce smaller, harder-to-detect shifts.

set.plain: Does it matter whether a coroner or a medical examiner investigates? It is not clear. In the US, medical examiners are usually doctors appointed to the job; coroners are often elected, and in some states need no medical training. In nine US states (2019 to 2021), deaths in coroner areas were more often recorded without saying whether the death was an accident or a suicide than deaths in medical examiner areas of the same state. Other studies found that certificates named no drug more often where coroners work. But seven states that switched to medical examiners showed no clear change in how precisely poisoning deaths were recorded, although that study could not rule out a real improvement, and its data end in 1998. Nobody checked which records were right.
set.magnitude: Nine US states 2019–2021, undetermined intent in coroner against medical-examiner counties (Lundberg et al., 2026): within state and year, odds ratio 1.79 (1.43–2.27); adjusted 1.52 (1.20–1.95), 1.61 (1.26–2.06), 1.60 (1.25–2.05); pooled without state, 0.32 (0.29–0.35), 558 of 18,232 (3.1%) against 3,329 of 37,198 (8.9%); no within-state contrast in Indiana, North Carolina or Maryland (editors' inference). Alcohol test recorded 58.6% against 84.5% (editors' percentages). Second-hand: unclassified overdose deaths in coroner counties, odds ratios 1.77 (1.08–2.90) in 2014 and 3.87 (2.32–6.46) in 2018 (Gutkind et al., 2025); undetermined manner varied by state but not by system, 2008–2010 (Gutkind et al., 2025); certificates naming specific drugs 92% (central medical examiner), 73% (hybrid), 71% (local medical examiner), 62% (coroner) (Slavova et al., 2015); undetermined share of drug poisoning deaths in 2016, 1% to 68% (Slavova et al., 2019). Seven state switches 1976–1996 (Zaychik, 2024): difference-in-differences in the non-specific share −0.02 (SE 0.04), −0.03 (0.05), −0.02 (0.06); editors' 95% intervals −0.10 to 0.06, −0.13 to 0.07, −0.14 to 0.10, probably too narrow (no stated allowance for repeated state-years). US offices 2018: about 80% in coroner systems (as quoted from the Bureau of Justice Statistics); toxicology access 75.1% (small) against 96.4% (large) (Smiley-McDonald et al., 2025).

evidence_set: As the review reports: Warner et al. (2013) found 85% of poisoning deaths in Maryland and over 40% in Utah classed as undetermined intent against 8% nationally; as of 2016 the share of drug poisoning deaths with undetermined intent still ranged from 1% (Connecticut, Massachusetts) to 68% (Maryland), and the authors suggest that medical examiner and coroner office policies not aligned with professional recommendations may influence this variation; the review does not name the states' system types here.

set.plain: Did news stories about mephedrone deaths get the facts right? Not always. In 2009 and 2010, online news in the UK linked 18 named deaths to mephedrone. Later reports said mephedrone was not found in 4 of them, was found but did not cause the death in 4, and played a part in 7, mostly together with other drugs or illnesses. The two deaths most linked to mephedrone online were later found to be from alcohol and methadone, and the first death in the news was reported as natural causes within a month. Online searches for mephedrone rose when deaths were in the news. The author thinks the news raised interest in the drug, but search data cannot show that the news made people use it. This comes from one study, and the later test results are second-hand reports, not official records.
